title: Black-hole singularities
part: IV: Orbits, stars, and black holes
one_line_summary: Separates genuine curvature singularities from artefacts of a bad coordinate choice, gives geodesic incompleteness and scalar invariants as the diagnostic tools, rehearses a null-ray-grid recipe on two disguised copies of flat spacetime (a 1/t^4 toy metric and Rindler), then applies it to Schwarzschild to build incoming and outgoing Eddington-Finkelstein coordinates, and uses the outgoing version to show that light from an infalling astronaut fades with an e-folding time of 4M.
role_in_book: Chapter 25 left the reader with a puzzle: in Schwarzschild coordinates an infalling astronaut takes infinite coordinate time to reach r = 2M, while her own clock records a finite plunge, and the tortoise coordinate pushed the horizon off to minus infinity. This chapter supplies the conceptual vocabulary (physical versus coordinate singularity, geodesic completeness, trapped surfaces) and the practical technique (null coordinates as a grid) needed to see through that puzzle. It deliberately stops at Eddington-Finkelstein coordinates, which fix only one family of light rays, so that Chapter 27 can complete the job with Kruskal-Szekeres coordinates and the full maximally extended geometry. A boxed note tells readers who want physics rather than coordinate technology that they can jump to Chapter 28 (Hawking radiation).

assumed_background.topic: Schwarzschild line element, the Schwarzschild radius r_S = 2M and geometrized units
Radial plunge orbits, conserved energy per unit mass from a time-independent metric, four-velocity normalization
Radial light rays in Schwarzschild and the gravitational redshift of photons
Tortoise coordinate r*, infinite coordinate time to reach r = 2M, the astronaut falling in and sending signals
Light-cone structure and null directions from ds^2 = 0 in Minkowski spacetime
Orthonormal-frame Riemann components of Schwarzschild and their tidal meaning
Raising and lowering indices with a metric and its matrix inverse
Coordinate transformations of a line element by substituting differentials
Plane polar coordinates and the cone as a surface
Integrating 1/(1 - 2M/r) and logarithms; hyperbolic functions; Taylor expansion near a point
Huygens-style wavefront envelopes of spherical light pulses

learning_objectives: Reader can explain the difference between a physical (curvature) singularity and a coordinate singularity, and give polar coordinates at the origin as a harmless example.
Reader can state why a diverging curvature scalar such as R_{abcd}R^{abcd} is convincing evidence of a real singularity while a diverging metric component is not.
Reader can define geodesic completeness and use incomplete geodesics as a working definition of a singular spacetime.
Reader can describe Penrose's closed trapped surface: a 2-sphere whose ingoing and outgoing light-front envelopes both have smaller area than the sphere itself.
Reader can show that ds^2 = -dt^2/t^4 + dx^2 is flat by substituting y = 1/t, and explain why its apparent problems at t = 0 and t = infinity come from bad labelling and incomplete coverage.
Reader can apply the null-grid recipe to Rindler spacetime: find the null curves, define u and v, rescale to U = -e^{-u}, V = e^{v}, and recognize Minkowski space covering only the wedge X > |T|.
Reader can derive the incoming Eddington-Finkelstein form of the Schwarzschild metric by substituting t = V - r*, and the outgoing form with t = U + r*.
Reader can find the two families of radial null curves in each Eddington-Finkelstein chart and say which family crosses r = 2M smoothly and which still looks singular there.
Reader can sketch light cones in incoming EF coordinates and describe how they tilt so that inside r = 2M every future direction heads to smaller r.
Reader can handle a non-diagonal metric: write g_{mu nu} for the (U, r) block, invert it, and raise indices correctly.

Reader can reproduce the argument that the received-to-emitted wavelength ratio equals dU/dtau of the infalling emitter, and derive the late-time exponential decay omega_infinity proportional to exp(-t/4M).
Reader can explain why Eddington-Finkelstein coordinates are an incomplete fix and why a chart regular for both ingoing and outgoing light (Kruskal-Szekeres) is needed.

teaching_approach.summary: A technical, recipe-building chapter framed by a physical hook. It opens with Penrose's trapped-surface picture to make singularities feel physical, then retreats to toy two-dimensional metrics where everything can be checked by hand: a polar-coordinate origin, a flat metric wearing a 1/t^4 disguise, and Rindler spacetime. Each toy is chosen to expose one idea (labelling failure, incomplete coverage, degenerate metric determinant) and together they rehearse a transferable algorithm: find the ingoing and outgoing null curves, use them as coordinates, and rescale until the metric looks like Minkowski light-cone form. The same algorithm is then run on a two-dimensional 'baby Schwarzschild' metric, paused halfway to extract Eddington-Finkelstein coordinates, and cashed out in a concrete physical calculation of the exponentially fading signal from a falling astronaut. The authors are explicit that the chapter is about coordinate technology and that the full cure is postponed to Chapter 27.
narrative_arc: Hook: Penrose (1965) trapped surfaces, where both ingoing and outgoing light fronts from a 2-sphere shrink, as a physical sign that something extreme sits inside.
Rough definition: a singularity is where a mathematical object misbehaves; near a true one no neighbourhood looks locally flat (cone apex).
Split singularities into physical and coordinate types; Example 26.1 shows polar coordinates failing at r = 0 while Cartesian ones are fine.
State the Schwarzschild verdict up front: r = 0 is physical (a curvature scalar diverges), r = 2M is a coordinate artefact (orthonormal Riemann components are finite there).
Sharpen the definition: geodesic completeness; a spacetime is singular if some geodesics cannot be extended in affine parameter.

Example 26.2: a flat metric in disguise; y = 1/t removes the t = 0 problem (points at infinity all labelled t = 0) and reveals that t -> infinity is merely the edge y = 0 of a half-plane that can be extended.
Announce the general strategy: use incoming and outgoing null geodesics as a coordinate grid.

Example 26.3 (Rindler): null curves t = +/- ln x give u, v; the metric becomes a conformal factor times -du dv; exponential rescaling gives exact Minkowski light-cone form; the original chart was only the wedge X > |T|.
Example 26.4: repeat the recipe on 2D Schwarzschild with the tortoise coordinate; ds^2 = -(1 - 2M/r) dU dV with r implicit.
Halfway house: keep r and one null coordinate to get incoming EF coordinates; metric acquires a dV dr cross term and loses its singularity at r = 2M.
Example 26.5: light cones in incoming EF coordinates; ingoing rays are straight and smooth, outgoing ones still singular at r_S; light at r = 2M hovers.
Example 26.6: collapsing star viewed in incoming EF coordinates; pulses reach a distant observer at growing intervals and stop once the surface passes r_S.
Introduce outgoing EF coordinates as the mirror image, regular for outgoing rays only.

Example 26.7: in outgoing EF coordinates, constancy of U along outgoing light turns the redshift problem into computing u^U of the plunging astronaut; expansion near r = 2M gives exponential fading with time constant 4M.
Wrap-up: the distant observer sees the astronaut slow and dim but EF coordinates still cannot cover everything; Kruskal-Szekeres coordinates are next.
signature_moves: Uses deliberately simple 2D toy metrics that turn out to be flat ('Minkowski space in disguise') so the learner can verify every claim before facing Schwarzschild.

Diagnoses each toy by a different symptom: coordinate labels collapsing (polar origin, t = 0), a chart covering only part of spacetime (t = infinity, Rindler wedge), and a vanishing metric determinant (Rindler at x = 0).

Turns 'inspired coordinate choices' into a stated recipe: null curves become coordinate lines, then reparametrize them until the metric is Minkowski light-cone form; an exercise then shows the rescaling can be derived from affine parameters instead of guessed.
Stops the Schwarzschild calculation halfway on purpose to harvest Eddington-Finkelstein coordinates as a 'halfway-house' chart, leaving the complete chart for the next chapter.

Makes the physical payoff of a clever coordinate explicit: because U is constant along outgoing light, pulse spacing in U is the same at emitter and receiver, reducing a redshift computation to one velocity component.
Places the reassuring curvature data (orthonormal Riemann components finite at r = 2M) and the reason scalars are trustworthy in margin notes, keeping the main line on coordinates.
Pairs each coordinate chart with a hand-drawn light-cone or pulse diagram (Figs 26.5-26.7) so the algebraic statement 'regular for ingoing rays only' is visible at a glance.

sections.title: Chapter opening: trapped surfaces
sections.summary: After a Blake epigraph about perception and a box saying the next two chapters are coordinate technicalities that can be skipped in favour of Chapter 28, the authors describe Penrose's 1965 construction. Every point of a large 2-sphere S emits a flash; the inward and outward envelopes of the flashes form spheres S1 and S2. Normally S1 is smaller and S2 larger than S, but with enough enclosed mass both are smaller, S is trapped and even outward light converges. A margin note tempers the implication: a trapped surface hints at, but does not guarantee, a singularity.
key_moves: Build the ingoing and outgoing wavefront envelopes from flashes emitted at every point of a sphere
Compare envelope areas with the original sphere; 'both smaller' is the trapped condition
Use the trapped surface as physical motivation for why locating genuine singularities requires care

sections.title: Singularities
sections.summary: Defines singularities roughly (a quantity misbehaves; no locally flat neighbourhood exists, as at a cone's apex), then separates physical singularities from coordinate singularities using polar coordinates at the origin. States that Schwarzschild has a physical singularity at r = 0, confirmed by a diverging curvature scalar, and a coordinate singularity at r = 2M, where the orthonormal-frame Riemann components quoted in a margin note stay finite. Introduces geodesic completeness and adopts incomplete geodesics as the robust definition of a singular spacetime. Two worked toys follow: a 1/t^4 metric that is flat after y = 1/t but covers only half of Minkowski space, and Rindler spacetime, whose null curves suggest coordinates that rescale to Minkowski light-cone form and reveal the chart as the wedge X > |T|.
key_moves: Cone apex as the picture of lost local flatness
Polar-coordinate origin: all values of theta label one point, yet Cartesian coordinates are regular
Scalars are coordinate independent, so a divergent scalar signals real trouble
Geodesic incompleteness as the working definition of a singularity
y = 1/t maps the toy metric to flat space; t = 0 is points at infinity, t -> infinity is the boundary y = 0 beyond which the space extends
Rindler: null curves t = +/- ln x, null coordinates u = t - ln x, v = t + ln x, metric -e^{v-u} du dv
Rescale U = -e^{-u}, V = e^{v}; ds^2 = -dU dV; then T, X recover -dT^2 + dX^2 and the Rindler chart is the wedge X > |T|

sections.title: Eddington-Finkelstein coordinates
sections.summary: Applies the null-grid recipe to the radial part of Schwarzschild. Null curves are t = +/- r*, giving U = t - r*, V = t + r* and ds^2 = -(1 - 2M/r) dU dV with r defined implicitly. Instead of finishing the job, the authors keep r and V (incoming EF) to get a metric with a 2 dV dr cross term that is regular at r = 2M. Light cones in this chart show ingoing rays as smooth straight lines and outgoing rays that escape only from outside r_S, hover at r_S, and fall inward from inside. A collapsing star is drawn in these coordinates, with pulses reaching a distant observer ever more slowly. Outgoing EF coordinates (r, U) are the mirror image. In them, a plunging astronaut's pulses travel along U = const, so the wavelength ratio equals dU/dtau at emission; evaluating u^U near r = 2M gives exponential redshift with time constant 4M. The chapter ends by noting that neither EF chart covers the full geometry.
concepts: exponential redshift of an infalling source
gravitational collapse to a black hole
key_moves: 2D baby-Schwarzschild null curves t = +/- r* and null coordinates U, V
ds^2 = -(1 - 2M/r) dU dV: conformal factor times Minkowski light-cone metric
Hybrid chart (V, r) via t = V - r* gives a metric with no singular coefficient at r = 2M
ds^2 = 0 factorizes into dV = 0 (ingoing) and dV = 2 dr/(1 - 2M/r) (outgoing)
Mirror construction t = U + r* for outgoing EF coordinates
Invert the non-diagonal (U, r) metric block and use normalization to solve for u_r, u^U, u^r
Constancy of U on outgoing light gives Delta U equal at emitter and receiver, so lambda_inf/lambda_em = dU/dtau
Near r = 2M, dU approx -4M d ln(r/2M - 1), so u^U grows like e^{U/4M} and received frequency decays like e^{-t/4M}

sections.title: Chapter summary and exercises
sections.summary: Two summary bullets: Schwarzschild has a physical singularity at r = 0 (associated with trapped surfaces) and a removable coordinate singularity at r_S; Eddington-Finkelstein coordinates remove it for ingoing or outgoing rays but not both. Four exercises follow on the curvature invariant, the EF metric determinant, the inverse metric, and deriving the Rindler rescaling from affine parameters.
key_moves: Condense the chapter into the physical/coordinate distinction plus the one-sided nature of EF coordinates
Exercise 26.4 replaces the guessed exponential rescaling with a derivation from affine parameters along null geodesics

concepts.name: spacetime singularity
concepts.definition: A place where spacetime cannot be described as a smooth Lorentzian manifold: curvature (as measured by coordinate-independent scalars) grows without bound, no neighbourhood is approximately flat, and freely falling observers or light rays reach it in finite affine parameter and cannot be continued. It is not a point of spacetime but an edge of it, and the known laws of physics give no prediction there.
concepts.how_introduced: First motivated physically by Penrose's trapped surfaces, then defined loosely as a spot where a mathematical object misbehaves, illustrated with the apex of a cone where no small patch looks flat, and finally sharpened to the geodesic-incompleteness criterion. The Schwarzschild r = 0 singularity is the flagship example.
concepts.notes: The book's rough and robust definitions are not reconciled in detail; a spacetime can be geodesically incomplete without curvature blowing up (e.g. a removed point, or conical defects), which the chapter does not discuss.

concepts.name: coordinate singularity
concepts.definition: A place where the components of the metric (or its inverse) written in a particular coordinate system become infinite, zero-determinant or otherwise ill-defined, although the geometry itself is smooth there; a different choice of coordinates removes the problem.
concepts.how_introduced: Contrasted with physical singularities and demonstrated with 2D polar coordinates, where every angle labels the same origin point, then with a 1/t^4 toy metric and Rindler spacetime. The Schwarzschild horizon r = 2M is named as the case the chapter must remove.
formulas: ds^2 = dr^2 + r^2 d\theta^2 = dx^2 + dy^2
concepts.notes: A margin note adds that coordinate singularities often force the use of several overlapping charts to cover a spacetime.

concepts.name: closed trapped surface
concepts.definition: A closed spacelike 2-surface (e.g. a sphere) such that both families of light rays emitted orthogonally from it, the inward-directed and the outward-directed, converge, so the areas of both future light-front envelopes are smaller than the area of the surface. In Schwarzschild every round sphere with r < 2M is trapped.
concepts.how_introduced: Penrose's 1965 construction opens the chapter: flashes from every point of a sphere form ingoing and outgoing envelope spheres S1 and S2; with sufficient mass inside, both shrink. Fig. 26.1 draws the construction.
concepts.notes: The book describes S as enclosing a large mass distribution and does not state that trapped spheres in Schwarzschild lie inside r = 2M. A footnote correctly warns that trapping suggests but does not by itself prove a singularity (the theorem needs further assumptions).

concepts.name: Penrose singularity theorem
concepts.definition: Result (Penrose 1965) that a spacetime containing a closed trapped surface, obeying the null energy condition and possessing a non-compact Cauchy surface, must contain at least one incomplete null geodesic.
concepts.how_introduced: Not named; alluded to through the trapped-surface opening and the footnote saying a trapped surface points toward, but does not guarantee, a singularity.
concepts.notes: Precise hypotheses are supplied here from standard literature, not from the book.

concepts.name: curvature invariant (Kretschmann scalar)
concepts.definition: The scalar formed by fully contracting the Riemann tensor with itself, K = R_{abcd}R^{abcd}. Being a scalar it takes the same value in every coordinate system, so if it diverges the curvature is genuinely infinite. For Schwarzschild K = 48M^2/r^6 (geometrized units), finite at r = 2M and divergent at r = 0.
concepts.how_introduced: Mentioned in the main text as the test that shows r = 0 is physical; a margin note explains that scalars are frame independent. Exercise 26.1 asks for its Schwarzschild value.
concepts.notes: Exercise 26.1 prints 12M^2/r^6, which is off by a factor of 4 (12 r_S^2/r^6 would be correct).

concepts.name: Schwarzschild Riemann components in an orthonormal frame
concepts.definition: The Schwarzschild Riemann tensor expressed in an orthonormal frame (the margin note labels its time direction tau-hat): magnitudes 2M/r^3 for the tau-r and theta-phi planes and M/r^3 for the tau-theta, tau-phi, r-theta and r-phi planes. The same values hold for a static observer and for a radially freely falling one, because a radial boost leaves these components unchanged. All are finite at r = 2M and diverge as r -> 0.
concepts.how_introduced: Recalled in footnote 4 next to the Schwarzschild metric; the note simply says 'orthonormal frame' and uses it as evidence that curvature is unremarkable at the horizon but blows up at the centre.
formulas: R_{\hat r\hat\theta\hat r\hat\theta} = R_{\hat r\hat\phi\hat r\hat\phi} = -\frac{M}{r^3}
concepts.notes: The page export mislabels the tau-hat indices as r-hat, producing an impossible R_{rrrr} and two conflicting R_{r theta r theta} lines; the PDF render shows tau-hat. Chapter 21 derives the same components with a t-hat label for static observers.

concepts.name: geodesic completeness
concepts.definition: A spacetime is geodesically complete if every geodesic x^mu(lambda) can be extended to all values of its affine parameter lambda. If some geodesic ends after a finite affine parameter at a point that is not part of the spacetime, the spacetime is geodesically incomplete, which is taken as the defining mark of a singular (or not fully extended) spacetime.
concepts.how_introduced: Offered as a sharper tool than 'something blows up', with Fig. 26.2 contrasting curves that continue indefinitely with a curve ending at a hatched blob. Used immediately in Example 26.2, where incompleteness at t -> infinity turns out to mean the chart can be extended rather than a true singularity.
concepts.notes: The example shows incompleteness alone does not tell you whether you face a real singularity or an extendable chart; the resolution is to find a larger spacetime into which the geodesics continue.

concepts.name: affine parameter
concepts.definition: A parameter lambda along a geodesic for which the geodesic equation takes its standard form with no extra term proportional to the tangent; it is unique up to lambda -> a lambda + b and, for timelike curves, can be proper time.
concepts.how_introduced: Relied upon in defining geodesic completeness, used via straight-line parametrizations in Example 26.2, and made central in Exercise 26.4, which derives the Rindler rescaling U = -e^{-u}, V = e^{v} from affine parameters of null geodesics.

concepts.name: local flatness
concepts.definition: In a smooth spacetime any sufficiently small region can be described by coordinates in which the metric is Minkowskian to first order; this fails at a curvature singularity.
concepts.how_introduced: Invoked negatively: at a physical singularity no patch is small enough to look flat, as with the apex of a cone.
concepts.notes: The cone is a slightly awkward example: its surface away from the apex is intrinsically flat, and the apex is a conical defect with delta-function curvature rather than smoothly diverging curvature.

concepts.name: light-cone (null) coordinates
concepts.definition: Coordinates u = t - x and v = t + x for 2D Minkowski spacetime, constant along outgoing and ingoing light rays respectively, in which the line element becomes ds^2 = -du dv (non-diagonal). More generally, any coordinates whose constant surfaces are null.
concepts.how_introduced: Recalled in a margin note from earlier light-cone work, then generalized to Rindler (u = t - ln x, v = t + ln x) and Schwarzschild (U = t - r*, V = t + r*).
formulas: u = t - x,\ v = t + x,\ ds^2 = -du\,dv

concepts.name: null-coordinate grid method
aliases: using null geodesics as a coordinate grid
removing coordinate singularities with null coordinates
concepts.definition: A procedure for removing coordinate singularities in (effectively) two-dimensional metrics: solve ds^2 = 0 for the ingoing and outgoing null curves, label each family by a constant to form null coordinates, write the metric as a conformal factor times -du dv, then reparametrize each null coordinate (ideally by an affine parameter along the rays) so the factor becomes regular and the chart extends across the former singular locus.
concepts.how_introduced: Announced after Example 26.2 as the sensible method behind seemingly magical coordinate choices, demonstrated fully on Rindler (Example 26.3), and applied partway to Schwarzschild (Example 26.4). Exercise 26.4 shows how affine parameters remove the guesswork.
concepts.notes: Works because in 2D ingoing and outgoing null curves never cross within their own family, giving a natural grid.

concepts.name: Rindler spacetime
concepts.definition: The 2D line element ds^2 = -x^2 dt^2 + dx^2 with x > 0. It is flat spacetime described by coordinates adapted to uniformly accelerated observers, covering only the wedge X > |T| of Minkowski spacetime; x = 0 is a coordinate singularity where the metric determinant vanishes, corresponding to the null lines X = |T|.
concepts.how_introduced: Example 26.3 treats it as a spacetime with an apparent singularity, applies the null-grid recipe, and shows it is Minkowski space; Fig. 26.4 shades the wedge. The accelerated-observer interpretation is not stressed here.
concepts.notes: Ideal rehearsal for Schwarzschild: the Rindler boundary X = |T| plays the role the horizon will play in Kruskal-Szekeres coordinates.

concepts.name: degenerate metric determinant
concepts.definition: If det g_{mu nu} = 0 at some locus, the inverse metric g^{mu nu} is undefined there, so index raising and equations of motion break down in that chart; this is a symptom of a coordinate or genuine singularity that must be tested further.
concepts.how_introduced: Given as the reason x = 0 looks singular in Rindler spacetime (g = -x^2 vanishes). Exercise 26.2 computes the EF determinant -r^4 sin^2 theta, which is non-zero at r = 2M.

concepts.name: extension of a spacetime
concepts.definition: Enlarging a spacetime described by a coordinate patch by embedding it in a bigger smooth spacetime into which its incomplete geodesics continue, typically by allowing new coordinates to take values that the old chart could not represent.
concepts.how_introduced: In Example 26.2 the half-plane y > 0 is extended by adding y <= 0; in Example 26.3 U and V are allowed to range over all reals rather than U < 0, V > 0, recovering all of Minkowski spacetime.
concepts.notes: The book does not point out explicitly that U = -e^{-u} is negative and V = e^v positive, so the original Rindler chart is the quadrant U < 0 < V; spelling this out makes the extension concrete.

concepts.name: Minkowski metric in disguise
concepts.definition: A line element that looks non-trivial or singular in some coordinates but becomes -dT^2 + dX^2 after a coordinate change, so its curvature vanishes identically and all its oddities are coordinate artefacts.
concepts.how_introduced: Both Example 26.2 and Example 26.3 end with the reveal that the strange metric was flat all along.

concepts.name: Schwarzschild metric
concepts.definition: The static, spherically symmetric vacuum solution ds^2 = -(1 - 2M/r)dt^2 + (1 - 2M/r)^{-1}dr^2 + r^2 dOmega^2 in geometrized units, singular in these coordinates at r = 2M (coordinate) and r = 0 (physical).
concepts.how_introduced: Recalled in a margin note together with its orthonormal Riemann components; its radial 2D part ('baby Schwarzschild') is the test case for the null-grid method.

concepts.name: event horizon
concepts.definition: The null surface r = 2M in Schwarzschild spacetime separating events that can send light to distant observers from those that cannot. Curvature is finite there, and in good coordinates it is an ordinary place that infalling matter crosses in finite proper time; outgoing light emitted exactly on it stays at r = 2M.
concepts.how_introduced: Stated to be a coordinate singularity of the Schwarzschild chart; its regularity is shown by EF coordinates, and its causal role by the tilted light cones and the collapsing-star pulses.

concepts.name: tortoise coordinate
concepts.definition: r* = r + 2M ln|r/2M - 1| (constant set to zero), chosen so that radial light rays in Schwarzschild satisfy t = +/- r* + const, i.e. dr*/dr = (1 - 2M/r)^{-1}; it maps r = 2M to r* = -infinity.
concepts.how_introduced: Recalled from Chapter 25 as the integral of the radial null condition in the baby-Schwarzschild example.

concepts.name: incoming Eddington-Finkelstein coordinates
concepts.definition: Coordinates for Schwarzschild spacetime that replace t by the ingoing null coordinate V = t + r* while keeping r, theta, phi. The metric -(1 - 2M/r)dV^2 + 2 dV dr + r^2 dOmega^2 is non-diagonal and regular (non-degenerate) at r = 2M, so ingoing light and infalling matter cross the horizon smoothly; outgoing rays still appear singular at r = 2M.
concepts.how_introduced: Presented as a 'halfway house' extracted from the null-grid construction for baby Schwarzschild, useful for anything falling into a black hole; illustrated by light cones (Fig. 26.5) and a collapsing star (Fig. 26.6).
concepts.notes: Plots use tbar = V - r as a timelike-looking vertical axis so ingoing rays are 45-degree lines.

concepts.name: outgoing Eddington-Finkelstein coordinates
concepts.definition: Coordinates for Schwarzschild spacetime using the outgoing null coordinate U = t - r* with r, theta, phi. The metric -(1 - 2M/r)dU^2 - 2 dU dr + r^2 dOmega^2 makes outgoing radial light (U = const) regular, while ingoing rays and infalling world lines appear singular at r = 2M; they describe the white-hole/exterior region naturally and are convenient for signals reaching distant observers.
concepts.how_introduced: Introduced as the mirror image of the incoming chart and put to work in Example 26.7 on the pulses of a falling astronaut (Fig. 26.7).
concepts.notes: The book prints the cross term as +2 dU dr in eqn 26.26, but its own matrix (26.28) and eqn 26.27 require -2 dU dr.

concepts.name: light-cone tilting at the horizon
concepts.definition: In horizon-penetrating coordinates the local light cones lean progressively toward decreasing r as r decreases: outside r = 2M one edge still points outward; at r = 2M the outgoing edge is vertical (light stays at fixed r); inside, both edges point to smaller r so every future-directed path ends at r = 0.
concepts.how_introduced: Example 26.5 solves ds^2 = 0 in incoming EF coordinates and Fig. 26.5 draws cones across the horizon; the text notes that light emitted outward at r = 2M neither escapes nor falls in.
concepts.notes: The book's phrase that at r = 2M 'V = r = const' is garbled: the stationary outgoing ray has r = 2M constant while V increases.

concepts.name: non-diagonal metric and index raising
concepts.definition: When the metric has cross terms (e.g. g_{Ur} = -1 with g_{rr} = 0), the inverse metric is not the componentwise reciprocal, and raising an index mixes components: u^U = g^{UU}u_U + g^{Ur}u_r, so a component with an upper index can depend on a different lower component entirely.
concepts.how_introduced: Flagged when the EF metric acquires a dV dr term (no dr^2 term) and worked concretely in Example 26.7 by writing the (U, r) block as a 2x2 matrix and inverting it; Exercises 26.2-26.3 practise it.

concepts.name: conserved energy per unit mass
concepts.definition: If the metric components do not depend on a coordinate, the corresponding covariant component of a geodesic's four-velocity is conserved. For Schwarzschild, E-tilde = -u_t; in EF coordinates the same quantity appears as -u_V or -u_U because t appears only through V or U.
concepts.how_introduced: A margin note on the incoming EF metric points out the absence of V dependence; Example 26.7 uses u_U = -E-tilde for a radial plunge.

concepts.name: four-velocity normalization
concepts.definition: For a massive particle parametrized by proper time, g^{mu nu}u_mu u_nu = -1; combined with conserved quantities it fixes the remaining velocity components.
concepts.how_introduced: Used in Example 26.7 with the inverse EF metric to obtain a quadratic for u_r.

concepts.name: radial plunge into a Schwarzschild black hole
concepts.definition: Radial timelike geodesic with conserved energy E-tilde, satisfying dr/dtau = -(E-tilde^2 - 1 + 2M/r)^{1/2}; it reaches r = 2M and then r = 0 in finite proper time, although Schwarzschild coordinate time diverges at the horizon.
concepts.how_introduced: The astronaut from Chapter 25 is revisited in outgoing EF coordinates; her four-velocity components are rederived there.

concepts.name: exponential redshift of an infalling source
concepts.definition: Signals emitted at regular proper-time intervals by an object falling through r = 2M reach a distant observer with frequency falling as exp(-t/4M) (and arrival rate likewise), so the object appears to slow, redden and fade exponentially quickly without ever being seen to cross. The time constant 4M = 4GM/c^3 is the inverse of the Schwarzschild surface gravity.
concepts.how_introduced: Qualitatively in Example 26.6 (collapsing star, growing gaps between received pulses) and quantitatively in Example 26.7 using outgoing EF coordinates: lambda_inf/lambda_em = dU/dtau, expanded near the horizon.
prerequisites: radial plunge into a Schwarzschild black hole
concepts.notes: The book does not name surface gravity (kappa = 1/4M); that link, and the same exponent's reappearance in Hawking temperature, is worth adding when teaching toward Chapter 28.

concepts.name: gravitational collapse to a black hole
concepts.definition: A star whose surface contracts through its Schwarzschild radius, forming a horizon; outside the surface the geometry is Schwarzschild, and in incoming EF coordinates the surface world line passes smoothly through r = 2M on its way to r = 0.
concepts.how_introduced: Example 26.6 and Fig. 26.6: an astronaut standing on the shrinking surface sends pulses outward, which reach the observer at growing intervals and cease once she is inside r_S.

concepts.name: Kruskal-Szekeres coordinates
concepts.definition: Coordinates obtained by completing the null-grid method for Schwarzschild (exponentially rescaled U and V) that are regular for both ingoing and outgoing light at r = 2M and cover the maximally extended Schwarzschild spacetime.
concepts.how_introduced: Only foreshadowed: the baby-Schwarzschild calculation is deliberately stopped before completion, and the chapter closes by saying the whole-geometry chart is the subject of Chapter 27.

key_equations.name: Plane polar line element
key_equations.meaning: Flat 2D metric in polar coordinates; at r = 0 the theta coordinate labels nothing new, a coordinate singularity removable by Cartesian coordinates.

key_equations.name: Schwarzschild metric (reminder)
key_equations.meaning: The metric whose singularities at r = 0 and r = 2M the chapter classifies.
key_equations.symbols: M mass (G = c = 1); t, r Schwarzschild coordinates

key_equations.name: Schwarzschild Riemann components in an orthonormal frame (footnote 4)
key_equations.latex: R_{\hat\tau\hat r\hat\tau\hat r} = -\frac{2M}{r^3},\ R_{\hat\theta\hat\phi\hat\theta\hat\phi} = \frac{2M}{r^3},\ R_{\hat\tau\hat\theta\hat\tau\hat\theta} = R_{\hat\tau\hat\phi\hat\tau\hat\phi} = \frac{M}{r^3},\ R_{\hat r\hat\theta\hat r\hat\theta} = R_{\hat r\hat\phi\hat r\hat\phi} = -\frac{M}{r^3}
key_equations.meaning: Measured tidal curvature is finite at r = 2M but diverges as r -> 0, supporting the physical/coordinate classification.
key_equations.symbols: hats denote orthonormal-frame components; tau-hat is the frame time direction (same values for static and radially infalling frames)

key_equations.name: Toy metric with apparent singularities
key_equations.meaning: A metric that looks bad at t = 0 and t = infinity; it is flat spacetime relabelled.

key_equations.name: Toy metric after y = 1/t
key_equations.meaning: Reveals Minkowski space; t = 0 is y -> infinity (points at infinity collapsed to one label), t -> infinity is the boundary y = 0.

key_equations.name: Straight-line geodesics in the toy spacetime (margin note 6)
key_equations.latex: y(\lambda) = m\lambda + c,\quad x = \lambda,\quad t = (m\lambda + c)^{-1}
key_equations.meaning: Geodesics continue indefinitely as t -> 0 but hit t -> +/- infinity at the finite parameter value lambda = -c/m, showing incompleteness of the original chart.
key_equations.symbols: m, c line constants; lambda affine parameter

key_equations.name: Minkowski light-cone coordinates (margin note 7)
key_equations.latex: u = t - x,\quad v = t + x,\quad ds^2 = -du\,dv
key_equations.meaning: Template metric form that the null-grid method aims for; outgoing light has u constant, ingoing light v constant.

key_equations.name: Rindler metric
key_equations.meaning: Metric with vanishing determinant at x = 0; flat spacetime in accelerated-observer coordinates.

key_equations.name: Rindler null condition
key_equations.meaning: Radial light rays from ds^2 = 0.

key_equations.name: Rindler null curves
key_equations.meaning: Plus sign outgoing, minus sign ingoing.

key_equations.name: Rindler null coordinates
key_equations.latex: u = t - \ln x,\quad v = t + \ln x
key_equations.meaning: Labels of outgoing and ingoing light rays used as coordinates.

key_equations.name: Rindler metric in null coordinates
key_equations.meaning: Conformal factor times the light-cone metric; u, v only cover x > 0.

key_equations.name: Exponential rescaling of null coordinates
key_equations.meaning: Absorbs the conformal factor; later shown (Exercise 26.4) to be affine parameters along the null rays.

key_equations.name: Rindler as Minkowski light-cone metric
key_equations.meaning: Flat and regular everywhere once U and V may take all real values.

key_equations.name: Inertial coordinates from U, V
key_equations.meaning: Undo the light-cone form to ordinary Minkowski coordinates.

key_equations.name: Rindler coordinates in terms of Minkowski coordinates
key_equations.meaning: Shows the Rindler chart is the wedge X > |T|; hyperbolae x = const are uniformly accelerated world lines and t is a boost rapidity.

key_equations.name: Flat metric recovered
key_equations.meaning: Rindler spacetime is flat.

key_equations.name: Two-dimensional Schwarzschild metric
key_equations.meaning: Radial (t, r) part used as the test case for the null-grid recipe.

key_equations.name: Radial null condition in Schwarzschild
key_equations.meaning: Coordinate slope of radial light rays; diverges at r = 2M.

key_equations.name: Radial null geodesics
key_equations.meaning: Light rays are 45-degree lines in (r*, t).

key_equations.name: Tortoise coordinate (margin note 10)
key_equations.meaning: Recalled from Chapter 25; constant set to zero.

key_equations.name: Schwarzschild null coordinates
key_equations.latex: U = t - r^*,\quad V = t + r^*
key_equations.meaning: Outgoing rays have U constant, ingoing rays V constant.

key_equations.name: 2D Schwarzschild in null coordinates
key_equations.meaning: Conformal factor times Minkowski light-cone metric, the stage at which Kruskal rescaling would follow.

key_equations.name: Implicit definition of r
key_equations.meaning: r must be recovered by inverting the tortoise relation.

key_equations.name: Incoming EF time substitution
key_equations.meaning: Replace Schwarzschild t by the ingoing null coordinate while keeping r.

key_equations.name: Schwarzschild metric in incoming Eddington-Finkelstein coordinates
key_equations.meaning: No coefficient blows up at r = 2M and the determinant is -r^4 sin^2 theta, so the chart extends smoothly through the horizon for infalling objects.

key_equations.name: Null condition in incoming EF
key_equations.meaning: Factorizes into ingoing (dV = 0) and outgoing solutions.

key_equations.name: Outgoing null direction in incoming EF
key_equations.meaning: dr/dV = (1 - 2M/r)/2: positive outside, zero at, negative inside the horizon.

key_equations.name: Outgoing rays in incoming EF
key_equations.meaning: Equivalent to V - 2r* = U = const; these curves still misbehave at r = 2M.

key_equations.name: Schwarzschild metric in outgoing Eddington-Finkelstein coordinates
key_equations.meaning: Regular for outgoing light; obtained with t = U + r*. Printed with +2 dU dr, which contradicts eqns 26.27-26.28; the minus sign shown here is correct.

key_equations.name: Ingoing null direction in outgoing EF
key_equations.meaning: Ingoing rays diverge in this chart at r = 2M, mirroring the incoming case.

key_equations.name: (U, r) metric block
key_equations.meaning: Non-diagonal metric with vanishing g_rr.

key_equations.name: Inverse (U, r) metric block
key_equations.meaning: g^{UU} = 0, so u^U depends only on u_r.

key_equations.name: Normalization with inverse EF metric
key_equations.meaning: Constraint for the plunging astronaut.

key_equations.name: Quadratic for u_r
key_equations.meaning: After substituting u_U = -E-tilde.
key_equations.symbols: E-tilde conserved energy per unit mass

key_equations.name: Covariant radial velocity
key_equations.meaning: The minus root is the infalling one: it gives u^r < 0 (the plus root would describe outward motion) and makes u^U diverge at the horizon. The text makes the choice without comment.

key_equations.name: U-component of four-velocity
key_equations.meaning: Rate of change of the outgoing null label along the world line; diverges at r = 2M.

key_equations.name: Radial four-velocity
key_equations.meaning: Same dr/dtau as in Schwarzschild coordinates, a consistency check (the print writes U_r for u_r in the first line).

key_equations.name: Wavelength ratio as pulse-interval ratio
key_equations.meaning: At fixed large r, Delta t equals Delta U.

key_equations.name: Redshift equals dU/dtau
key_equations.meaning: Because U is constant along each outgoing pulse, the redshift is simply u^U at emission.

key_equations.name: Trajectory slope in (U, r)
key_equations.meaning: Relates the astronaut's radius to the retarded time label; near r = 2M it reduces to -(1 - 2M/r)/2.

key_equations.name: Near-horizon expansion
key_equations.meaning: Leading behaviour as r -> 2M.

key_equations.name: Logarithmic approach in U
key_equations.meaning: The astronaut reaches r = 2M only as U -> infinity.

key_equations.name: Exponential approach to the horizon
key_equations.meaning: Up to a multiplicative constant (the print uses approx for a proportionality).

key_equations.name: Exponential growth of u^U
key_equations.meaning: Received wavelength grows exponentially in the retarded time.

key_equations.name: Late-time redshift law
key_equations.meaning: Distant observers see the infalling source's frequency decay exponentially with time constant 4M (4GM/c^3).
key_equations.symbols: t proper time of the distant observer

key_equations.name: Kretschmann scalar of Schwarzschild (as printed in Exercise 26.1)
key_equations.meaning: Finite at r = 2M, infinite at r = 0; the standard value is 48M^2/r^6 = 12 r_S^2/r^6, so the printed coefficient is wrong by a factor 4 (the conclusion is unaffected).

key_equations.name: Rindler conserved quantity along null geodesics (Exercise 26.4)
key_equations.meaning: t does not appear in the Rindler metric, so -g_{tt} dt/dlambda is constant.

key_equations.name: Affine parameter on outgoing Rindler rays (Exercise 26.4)
key_equations.meaning: At fixed u, e^v is an affine parameter, justifying V = e^v; similarly -e^{-u} on ingoing rays.

figures.label: Fig. 26.1
figures.caption_paraphrase: Penrose's trapped-surface construction: a sphere is trapped when the envelopes of both its ingoing and outgoing light fronts have less area than it does.
figures.visual_description: Line drawing of concentric circles in cross-section. A middle circle labelled S carries three marked emission points (one labelled P). Around each point is a small circle (one labelled T) representing the light front a little later. An inner concentric circle S1 is tangent to the inner sides of the small circles and an outer concentric circle S2 is tangent to their outer sides. The drawing shows the normal (untrapped) flat-space situation, with S1 smaller and S2 larger than S.
figures.what_it_teaches: How ingoing and outgoing wavefront envelopes are built from a sphere of flashes, setting up the idea that strong gravity can make even the outer envelope shrink.

redesign.idea: Trapped-sphere slider: a ring of emitters on a sphere of areal radius r around mass M launches flashes; ingoing and outgoing envelopes are drawn with areas computed from the Schwarzschild expansion rates, with the outer envelope's area bar turning red when it drops below the original.
redesign.interaction: Drag r/2M from 3 down to 0.5 (or dial M at fixed r); scrub time; toggle between a flat-space view and a curved-spacetime view; readouts show d(area)/d(lambda) for both families.

figures.label: Fig. 26.2
figures.caption_paraphrase: Left: a geodesic that can be extended endlessly in both directions (complete). Right: a geodesic that runs into a hatched singular region and cannot be continued (incomplete).
figures.visual_description: Two side-by-side panels labelled (a) and (b), each showing a single bold wavy curve rising from lower left to upper right. In (a) both ends fade into dotted continuations, indicating the curve goes on. In (b) the lower end is dotted but the upper end terminates at a small cross-hatched disc.
figures.what_it_teaches: The geodesic-completeness criterion for singularities in pictorial form: singular means some freely falling path ends after finite affine parameter.

redesign.idea: Affine-parameter odometer: launch geodesics in several 2D spacetimes (flat plane, cone with apex, half-plane chart of the toy metric, Schwarzschild interior) and watch an odometer of affine parameter; a geodesic that stops at a finite odometer reading is flagged incomplete, and the app asks whether the stop is an extendable chart edge or a true singularity.
redesign.interaction: Choose spacetime from a menu, click to set a launch point and direction, press play; toggle 'extend chart' to see whether the curve continues into an added region.

figures.label: Fig. 26.3
figures.caption_paraphrase: The region of flat spacetime reached by the toy coordinates of eqn 26.3 is only the upper half y > 0; the lower half must be added to complete Minkowski space.
figures.visual_description: Cartesian axes with x horizontal and y vertical (arrows labelled x and y, origin labelled 0). The entire strip above the x axis is shaded grey; the region below the axis is white.
figures.what_it_teaches: A metric can look singular at a coordinate boundary simply because the chart covers only part of a perfectly regular spacetime.

redesign.idea: Two linked panels: the original t-x chart (with t on a log scale) and the y-x Minkowski plane. Straight geodesics drawn in the y-x plane are mapped into the t-x panel, where they rush off to t = infinity at y = 0 and pile up toward t = 0 as y grows.
redesign.interaction: Drag a geodesic's slope and intercept in the Minkowski panel; a marker moving along it shows the corresponding t value; a button 'extend' reveals the y < 0 half-plane.

figures.label: Fig. 26.4
figures.caption_paraphrase: Rindler coordinates cover only the right-hand wedge of Minkowski spacetime between the two light lines through the origin.
figures.visual_description: Minkowski diagram with X horizontal and T vertical. Two diagonal lines through the origin (T = X and T = -X) divide the plane into four quadrants. The right-hand wedge, X > |T|, is shaded grey.
figures.what_it_teaches: The apparent singularity of Rindler at x = 0 is the edge of the wedge, the light lines X = |T|, beyond which ordinary Minkowski space continues; it rehearses the horizon structure of Kruskal diagrams.

redesign.idea: Rindler grid overlay: draw constant-x hyperbolae and constant-t rays inside the wedge, plus the u, v null lines, and show how the U = -e^{-u}, V = e^{v} map stretches them into the full Minkowski grid.
redesign.interaction: Slider morphs between (t, x) rectangular grid, (u, v) grid and (U, V)/(T, X) Minkowski picture; hover a point to read all coordinate values; toggle to show world lines of accelerated observers (x = const).

figures.label: Fig. 26.5
figures.caption_paraphrase: Light cones drawn in incoming Eddington-Finkelstein coordinates, with vertical axis tbar = V - r against r.
figures.visual_description: Vertical axis tbar, horizontal axis r, with a wavy vertical line at r = 0 marking the singularity and a bold vertical line at r = 2M. A family of parallel dashed straight lines runs diagonally down-left at 45 degrees (ingoing rays), one of them drawn heavier near the bottom where it meets r = 0. Another family of dashed curves rises steeply on the right and bends: outside 2M they tilt outward and flatten away, near 2M they hug the vertical line, and inside they curve toward r = 0. Small cone-shaped symbols are drawn at many points; far out they are symmetric about the vertical, nearer the horizon they lean toward decreasing r, and inside 2M they point entirely toward the singularity.
figures.what_it_teaches: The horizon is locally unremarkable for ingoing light, but the causal structure tips over so that inside r = 2M every future path heads to r = 0; also shows outgoing rays still bunching at 2M in this chart.

redesign.idea: Live light-cone field: compute and draw the null cone from eqn 26.24 at a movable probe point, with a trail of outgoing and ingoing rays integrated from it; companion panel shows the same rays in Schwarzschild (t, r) coordinates where they blow up at 2M.
redesign.interaction: Drag the probe across r = 2M; slider for mass M; toggle coordinate chart (Schwarzschild, incoming EF, outgoing EF); click to fire a photon or a massive particle with chosen energy.

figures.label: Fig. 26.6
figures.caption_paraphrase: A star collapses in incoming Eddington-Finkelstein coordinates while a person on its surface sends light outward toward a distant observer.
figures.visual_description: Axes tbar (vertical) and r (horizontal). The star is a region filled with horizontal hatching at the bottom left, labelled 'star'; its surface is a curve that starts at moderate r on the r axis and sweeps up and inward to reach r = 0 about halfway up the plot. A vertical solid line labelled 'horizon' rises from the point where the surface passes r = 2M. Above the point where the surface reaches the centre, a wavy vertical line at r = 0 is labelled 'singularity', and the strip between it and the horizon line is filled with diagonal hatching. A dashed vertical line further right is labelled 'observer'. Long-dashed outgoing light curves leave the stellar surface outside the horizon: the early ones lean well over to the right, and those launched closer to r = 2M rise ever more steeply, hugging the horizon line before peeling away toward the observer. No rays are drawn leaving the surface once it is inside the horizon.
figures.what_it_teaches: Collapse and horizon formation look smooth in a horizon-penetrating chart, while distant observers receive the signals ever more slowly and eventually not at all.
concepts: gravitational collapse to a black hole
exponential redshift of an infalling source

redesign.idea: Collapse-and-beacon simulator: the stellar surface follows a free-fall trajectory in incoming EF coordinates and emits pulses at equal proper-time ticks; each pulse is ray-traced to an observer at chosen radius, with a synchronized strip chart of arrival times and received frequency.
redesign.interaction: Play/pause and scrub the astronaut's proper time; set emission rate, initial radius and observer distance; watch arrival gaps grow exponentially and the last escaping pulse highlighted.

figures.label: Fig. 26.7
figures.caption_paraphrase: A falling astronaut emits light pulses, drawn in outgoing Eddington-Finkelstein coordinates with tbar = U + r.
figures.visual_description: Small axis arrows show tbar up and r to the right. A curved world line, labelled r(tau) at its lower end, climbs from lower right toward upper left as the astronaut moves to smaller r. Four parallel straight lines leave points on the world line and rise at 45 degrees to the right; one is labelled 'U = const.' They end on a vertical line at the right, marked 'obs' at the top and with an infinity sign at the bottom, representing the distant receiver. The sketch is schematic: it shows that emission-point spacing in U is copied to the receiver, not the quantitative growth of the gaps.
figures.what_it_teaches: Outgoing light rays are straight lines of constant U in this chart, so the spacing of pulses in U is carried unchanged from emitter to distant receiver, turning redshift into a single derivative dU/dtau.
concepts: exponential redshift of an infalling source

redesign.idea: Pulse-spacing ruler: the plunge world line in (U, r) with equally spaced proper-time beads; 45-degree pulse lines carry the U spacing to the observer; a log-scale plot beside it shows Delta U per tick versus U with the fitted slope 1/4M.
redesign.interaction: Slide E-tilde (drop from rest vs thrown in) and M; scrub tau; toggle log axis to reveal the straight-line exponential regime and read off the e-folding time.

worked_examples.label: Example 26.1
worked_examples.problem: Decide whether the breakdown of plane polar coordinates at r = 0 is a real feature of the plane.
worked_examples.method: Note that at r = 0 every theta gives the same point, so the coordinates stop labelling uniquely; rewrite the metric in Cartesian coordinates, where nothing special happens at the origin.
worked_examples.key_insight: Coordinates can fail while the geometry stays perfectly smooth; a change of chart exposes the difference.
worked_examples.result: r = 0 is a coordinate singularity; ds^2 = dx^2 + dy^2 is regular there.

worked_examples.label: Example 26.2
worked_examples.problem: Analyse the metric ds^2 = -dt^2/t^4 + dx^2, which looks troublesome both at t = 0 and as t -> infinity.
worked_examples.method: Substitute y = 1/t to obtain the Minkowski metric; interpret t = 0 as the collection of points at y -> infinity; use straight-line geodesics y = m x + c parametrized by x to show completeness toward t = 0 but a finite-parameter end at t -> infinity (y = 0); extend by adjoining y <= 0.
worked_examples.key_insight: Two different coordinate pathologies coexist: many distinct points squeezed onto one label (t = 0) and a chart that stops at a boundary where geodesics end (t = infinity). Geodesic incompleteness in a chart can signal that the spacetime should be extended, not that it is singular.
worked_examples.result: The spacetime is flat half-Minkowski (y > 0) and extends to all of Minkowski space; no genuine singularity.

worked_examples.label: Example 26.3
worked_examples.problem: Show that Rindler spacetime ds^2 = -x^2 dt^2 + dx^2, whose metric determinant vanishes at x = 0, is free of genuine singularities.
worked_examples.method: Solve ds^2 = 0 to get null curves t = +/- ln x; define u = t - ln x, v = t + ln x giving ds^2 = -e^{v-u} du dv; guess the rescaling U = -e^{-u}, V = e^v to get -dU dV; allow U, V over all reals; transform to T = (U+V)/2, X = (V-U)/2.
worked_examples.key_insight: Null rays form a natural grid; after reparametrizing them the metric is manifestly Minkowski, and the original chart covers only X > |T|.
worked_examples.result: ds^2 = -dT^2 + dX^2 with x = sqrt(X^2 - T^2), t = artanh(T/X); x = 0 corresponds to the null lines X = |T|.

worked_examples.label: Example 26.4
worked_examples.problem: Run the Rindler recipe on the two-dimensional (t, r) part of the Schwarzschild metric.
worked_examples.method: Set ds^2 = 0 to get (dt/dr)^2 = (1 - 2M/r)^{-2}; integrate to t = +/- r*; define U = t - r*, V = t + r*; substitute to obtain -(1 - 2M/r) dU dV with r given implicitly by r* = (V - U)/2.
worked_examples.key_insight: Schwarzschild's radial part has the same structure as Rindler: a conformal factor times the light-cone metric. The factor vanishes at r = 2M, which is what a further rescaling must fix; the authors pause here to extract EF coordinates.
worked_examples.result: ds^2 = -(1 - 2M/r) dU dV, with r + 2M ln|r/2M - 1| = (V - U)/2.

worked_examples.problem: Rewrite the full Schwarzschild metric using the ingoing null coordinate V in place of t (embedded derivation).
worked_examples.method: Substitute t = V - r*, so dt = dV - dr/(1 - 2M/r); expand -(1 - 2M/r)dt^2 + (1 - 2M/r)^{-1}dr^2 and observe the dr^2 terms cancel.
worked_examples.key_insight: The singular dr^2 coefficient is traded for a harmless cross term; the metric is regular at r = 2M.

worked_examples.label: Example 26.5
worked_examples.problem: Find the radial light cones of Schwarzschild in incoming Eddington-Finkelstein coordinates.
worked_examples.method: Set ds^2 = 0 in the (V, r) metric, factor out dV to get dV = 0 or -(1 - 2M/r)dV + 2 dr = 0, and integrate the second.
worked_examples.key_insight: Ingoing rays are smooth straight lines through the horizon; outgoing rays escape from r > 2M, stay put at r = 2M, and fall inward from r < 2M.
worked_examples.result: Ingoing: V = const. Outgoing: V - 2(r + 2M ln|r/2M - 1|) = const.

worked_examples.label: Example 26.6
worked_examples.problem: Describe what a distant observer receives from an astronaut on the surface of a collapsing star, using incoming EF coordinates.
worked_examples.method: Draw the shrinking stellar surface in (tbar, r) and follow outgoing light pulses along curves V - 2r* = const to the observer (qualitative, Fig. 26.6).
worked_examples.key_insight: The surface crosses the horizon smoothly in this chart, while received pulse intervals stretch without limit and pulses emitted inside never escape.
worked_examples.result: Growing gaps between received pulses; no pulses after the surface passes r_S.
concepts: gravitational collapse to a black hole
exponential redshift of an infalling source

worked_examples.problem: Construct outgoing Eddington-Finkelstein coordinates and find their radial null directions (embedded calculation).
worked_examples.method: Substitute t = U + r* into Schwarzschild, then set ds^2 = 0 and factor.
worked_examples.key_insight: Mirror image of the incoming chart: outgoing rays (U = const) are regular, ingoing rays have dU/dr = -2/(1 - 2M/r), singular at 2M.
worked_examples.result: ds^2 = -(1 - 2M/r)dU^2 - 2 dU dr + r^2 dOmega^2 (printed with +2 dU dr, a sign slip).

worked_examples.label: Example 26.7
worked_examples.problem: An astronaut plunging radially into a Schwarzschild black hole emits pulses at equal proper-time intervals; find how the frequency received by a distant observer evolves at late times.
worked_examples.method: Work in outgoing EF coordinates. Use U-independence to set u_U = -E-tilde; invert the (U, r) metric block; impose normalization to get a quadratic for u_r and choose the root; raise indices to find u^U and u^r. Because outgoing pulses keep U fixed, the wavelength ratio equals dU/dtau = u^U at emission. Form dr/dU = u^r/u^U, expand near r = 2M, integrate to U approx -4M ln(r/2M - 1), and substitute back; at large r, U differs from t by a constant.
worked_examples.key_insight: Choosing coordinates constant along the signal's path turns a propagation problem into a local one: redshift is simply the rate at which the emitter's outgoing-null label advances.
worked_examples.result: u^U proportional to e^{U/4M}, so omega_inf/omega_em approx e^{-t/4M}: exponential fading with time constant 4M, and infinite redshift in the limit.
concepts: exponential redshift of an infalling source
radial plunge into a Schwarzschild black hole

analogies_and_intuitions.how_used: Invites the reader to imagine shrinking a patch around the apex of a cone: however small, it never looks like a flat sheet, which is the sense in which smoothness is lost at a genuine singularity.
analogies_and_intuitions.limits: A cone is flat everywhere except the apex, and its apex has concentrated rather than diverging curvature; Schwarzschild's r = 0 has tidal curvature growing without bound as it is approached, and is not a point in spacetime at all.
analogies_and_intuitions.app_idea: Zoom-in test: repeatedly magnify a region of a surface (sphere, saddle, cone apex, cone flank) and overlay a flat grid; the flat grid fits better on each zoom except at the apex.

analogies_and_intuitions.how_used: Every angle points at the same origin, so angle loses meaning there, yet nothing is wrong with the plane; Cartesian coordinates prove it. The Schwarzschild horizon is presented as the same kind of labelling failure.
analogies_and_intuitions.limits: At the polar origin a whole circle of labels collapses to a point; at r = 2M the problem is instead that Schwarzschild t runs off to infinity along infalling paths, a different mechanism. Learners may over-generalize and assume every coordinate problem is removable.
analogies_and_intuitions.app_idea: Drag a point toward the origin in polar and Cartesian readouts simultaneously; the theta readout jitters wildly near the origin while x, y change smoothly. A second tab does the same for an infalling particle with Schwarzschild t versus EF V readouts.

analogies_and_intuitions.analogy: A familiar spacetime wearing a disguise
analogies_and_intuitions.how_used: Both toy metrics are unmasked as flat space; the narrative tone ('flat space all along') trains the reader to suspect coordinates before blaming geometry.
analogies_and_intuitions.limits: Schwarzschild is not flat in disguise: its curvature is real. Only the horizon behaviour is a disguise.
analogies_and_intuitions.app_idea: 'Unmask the metric' game: present an odd-looking 2D metric, let the learner try substitutions from a palette, and reward them when the metric morphs to -dT^2 + dX^2; include a Schwarzschild card that can be made regular at 2M but never flat.

analogies_and_intuitions.how_used: In two dimensions the ingoing rays never cross one another, and likewise the outgoing rays, so the two families form a ready-made grid; labelling the grid lines gives coordinates adapted to causality.
analogies_and_intuitions.limits: Only clean in 2D or for radial motion in spherical symmetry; in general 4D spacetimes null congruences can cross (caustics) and a grid does not exist globally.
analogies_and_intuitions.app_idea: Draw ingoing and outgoing ray families in a chosen 2D metric and let the learner relabel them with arbitrary monotone functions until the grid cells look like diamonds of equal size.

analogies_and_intuitions.how_used: EF coordinates are framed as a stopping point partway to the full solution, keeping one ordinary coordinate (r) and one null coordinate, which is enough for one-way traffic through the horizon.
analogies_and_intuitions.limits: The metaphor hides that the chart covers a genuinely different region (black hole or white hole interior) depending on which null coordinate is kept.

analogies_and_intuitions.analogy: Watching someone slow down and fade from a safe distance
analogies_and_intuitions.target_concept: exponential redshift of an infalling source
analogies_and_intuitions.how_used: Closes Example 26.7 with the image of a distant observer seeing the astronaut simultaneously slow and dim as she nears r_S, reconciling finite proper time with infinite coordinate time.
analogies_and_intuitions.limits: The picture suggests she remains visible forever; in practice after a few multiples of 4M the signal is undetectable, and a real photon count becomes finite.
analogies_and_intuitions.app_idea: Split screen: astronaut's own view with steady clock ticks versus distant telescope view where image colour reddens and brightness drops on a log scale with e-folding 4M.

analogies_and_intuitions.how_used: Fig. 26.5 lets the reader see causality change: cones lean inward until, inside 2M, the future lies entirely toward smaller r.
analogies_and_intuitions.limits: The amount of tilt is chart dependent; in Schwarzschild coordinates cones instead narrow to slivers. Only the invariant statement (future of r < 2M reaches smaller r) is physical.
analogies_and_intuitions.app_idea: Flow field of cones that the learner can switch between charts, with a caption stating which features survive a change of coordinates.

analogies_and_intuitions.analogy: Expanding and contracting ripples from a ring of flashes
analogies_and_intuitions.how_used: Builds intuition for trapping from the everyday picture that light fronts from a sphere form a smaller inner and larger outer envelope, then reverses the expectation for the outer one.
analogies_and_intuitions.limits: The flat-space envelope picture cannot show why the outer envelope shrinks; that requires curved-spacetime focusing, which the book asserts rather than derives.

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: The event horizon at r = 2M is a physical singularity where something infinite or destructive happens.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: Curvature scalars and orthonormal tidal components are finite at r = 2M; the breakdown is in Schwarzschild coordinates, and EF coordinates cross it smoothly.
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: The Schwarzschild metric components blow up or vanish there, and popular language treats the horizon as the 'edge' of the black hole.

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: If some metric component becomes infinite, the physics must break down there.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: Components depend on the coordinates; only coordinate-independent quantities (scalars, geodesic behaviour) can certify a genuine singularity.
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: In earlier chapters components were treated as 'the metric', and infinities in formulas feel physical.

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: A metric that looks complicated or singular must describe curved spacetime.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: Both -dt^2/t^4 + dx^2 and -x^2 dt^2 + dx^2 are flat Minkowski space in unusual coordinates.
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: The form of a line element is the most visible feature, and learners judge curvature by appearance.

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: When geodesics stop at the edge of a chart, the spacetime has a singularity there.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: Geodesic incompleteness in a given chart may only mean the chart covers part of a larger spacetime; one must try to extend it (adding y <= 0, or letting U and V range over all reals) before declaring a singularity.
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: Geodesic incompleteness was just offered as the definition of a singularity.

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: One coordinate system should be able to describe an entire spacetime.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: Coordinate singularities often force several overlapping charts; neither EF chart covers all of Schwarzschild, motivating Kruskal-Szekeres coordinates.
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: Flat-space experience with global Cartesian coordinates.

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: Because a distant observer never sees the astronaut reach the horizon, she never crosses it.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: In incoming EF coordinates infalling world lines pass r = 2M continuously in finite proper time; the distant view freezes only because signals from near the horizon are delayed and redshifted exponentially.
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: Infinite Schwarzschild coordinate time from Chapter 25 is easily mistaken for infinite physical time.
concepts: exponential redshift of an infalling source
radial plunge into a Schwarzschild black hole

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: Finding a trapped surface proves a singularity exists.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: A trapped surface strongly suggests a singularity but the implication needs extra assumptions (energy conditions and global structure, as in Penrose's theorem).
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: The chapter opening presents trapping as caused by the central singularity.

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: Eddington-Finkelstein coordinates fully remove the horizon problem.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: Each EF chart regularizes only one family of radial light rays; the other still looks singular at r = 2M.
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: The incoming EF metric has no singular coefficient at r = 2M, which looks like complete success.

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: 'Outgoing' light emitted inside the horizon still moves to larger r, just slowly.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: Inside r = 2M the so-called outgoing rays also move to smaller r and hit r = 0; at exactly r = 2M they stay at fixed r.
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: The name 'outgoing' and the flat-space habit that one light-cone edge always points outward.

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: With a non-diagonal metric you can still raise an index by dividing by the diagonal component.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: Invert the full matrix; in outgoing EF, g^{UU} = 0 and g^{Ur} = -1, so u^U = -u_r and u^r mixes u_U and u_r.
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: All metrics met previously (Minkowski, Schwarzschild, FRW) were diagonal.

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: The astronaut herself sees her signals redden or her clock slow as she approaches the horizon.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: The exponential redshift is what the distant receiver measures; locally the astronaut's clock and emission frequency are normal.
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: The chapter describes the effect vividly without always specifying whose measurement it is.
concepts: exponential redshift of an infalling source

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: A diverging component of the Riemann tensor in some frame is enough to establish a curvature singularity.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: Components can blow up because of a bad frame; a divergent scalar (or divergent components in a frame carried by a physical observer) is what counts.
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: The margin note lists orthonormal components that diverge at r = 0, which could be read as the proof.

thought_experiments.name: Flashes from every point of a sphere (Penrose)
thought_experiments.setup: A 2-sphere surrounds a concentration of mass; at one instant every point on it emits a flash, and one follows the inner and outer envelopes of the flashes.
thought_experiments.lesson: In weak gravity the outer envelope grows; with enough gravity both envelopes shrink, so light aimed outward is still dragged inward, the hallmark of a trapped region.
thought_experiments.app_idea: 3D sphere of emitters with ingoing and outgoing shells whose radii follow the Schwarzschild radial null equations; slider moves the sphere across r = 2M.

thought_experiments.name: Astronaut beaconing from a collapsing star
thought_experiments.setup: Someone stands on the surface of a star collapsing into a black hole, sending regular light pulses to a distant observer.
thought_experiments.lesson: The distant observer receives pulses at ever longer intervals and then no more once the surface is inside r_S, even though the surface crosses the horizon smoothly.
concepts: gravitational collapse to a black hole
thought_experiments.app_idea: Tie to the Fig. 26.6 redesign: a counter at the observer listing arrival times of pulses 1, 2, 3, ... and the last one that ever arrives.

thought_experiments.name: Radio pulses from a plunging astronaut
thought_experiments.setup: The Chapter 25 astronaut falls radially and emits pulses at equal intervals of her proper time; a distant observer records their arrival times and frequencies.
thought_experiments.lesson: Received frequency decays exponentially with time constant 4M, so she appears to freeze and fade; the coordinate choice makes the calculation almost trivial.
concepts: exponential redshift of an infalling source
thought_experiments.app_idea: Sound-based demo: each received pulse plays a tone whose pitch and loudness follow the computed redshift, so the learner hears the exponential drop.

thought_experiments.name: Chasing a geodesic to the edge of a chart
thought_experiments.setup: In the toy spacetime -dt^2/t^4 + dx^2, follow a straight geodesic by increasing and decreasing its parameter and watch t.
thought_experiments.lesson: One direction runs forever toward t = 0, the other reaches t = infinity at finite parameter, revealing that the chart ends where the spacetime does not.

historical_notes.event: Introduced closed trapped surfaces in analysing the interior of black holes and gravitational collapse.
historical_notes.significance: Provided a coordinate-free, physical criterion linked to singularity formation, later central to his singularity theorem (and cited in his 2020 Nobel Prize, context not in book).

historical_notes.event: Namesake of Eddington-Finkelstein coordinates; a margin biography notes his quantum-gravity work, research on ball lightning, an analysis of Durer's engraving Melencolia I, and his coining of the name 'sine-Gordon model' as a pun he later regretted.
historical_notes.significance: Humanizes the coordinates; historically (not stated in the book) Finkelstein's 1958 use of these coordinates clarified that r = 2M is a one-way membrane, following Eddington's 1924 form of the transformation.

applications_and_observations.topic: Fading of matter falling into a black hole
applications_and_observations.details: The late-time redshift law omega proportional to exp(-t/4M) implies that light from infalling gas or a collapsing stellar surface dims and reddens on a timescale 4GM/c^3. Our own estimates for representative masses follow.
applications_and_observations.key_numbers: Time constant 4GM/c^3 approx 20 microseconds for 1 solar mass, 0.2 ms for 10 solar masses, about 85 s for Sgr A* (4.3 million solar masses), about 1.5 days for M87* (6.5 billion solar masses). (Our estimates; not in book.)

applications_and_observations.topic: Tidal curvature at the horizon versus at the centre
applications_and_observations.details: Since orthonormal curvature components scale as M/r^3, the tidal stretching at r = 2M is c^6/(4G^2M^2), which shrinks with black-hole mass, while it diverges as r -> 0 for any mass. This quantifies the book's statement that the horizon is locally ordinary.
applications_and_observations.key_numbers: Radial tidal gradient 2GM/r^3 at r_S: about 1e8 s^-2 for 10 solar masses (lethal spaghettification before reaching the horizon); about 5.6e-4 s^-2 for Sgr A* (unnoticeable). Kretschmann scalar at r_S is 3/(4M^4) in geometrized units. (Our estimates; not in book.)

applications_and_observations.topic: Gravitational collapse of a star seen from outside
applications_and_observations.details: Example 26.6 sketches a star whose surface falls through r_S; outside observers see pulses arrive progressively later and then stop, which is the classical picture behind a 'frozen star' and the rapid effective blackening of collapsing objects.

notation_and_conventions.convention: Geometrized units G = c = 1; Schwarzschild radius r_S = 2M; time constant 4M means 4GM/c^3 in SI.
(-, +, +, +); timelike intervals have ds^2 < 0 and four-velocity satisfies u.u = -1.
Components in an orthonormal frame; the margin note writes the time direction as tau-hat.
notation_and_conventions.notes: The page export renders tau-hat as r-hat; the PDF render confirms tau-hat. Chapter 21 uses t-hat for the same components.

notation_and_conventions.convention: Lowercase u = t - x, v = t + x (Minkowski) and u = t - ln x, v = t + ln x (Rindler); uppercase U, V are used both for the exponentially rescaled Rindler coordinates (U = -e^{-u}, V = e^v) and for the Schwarzschild null coordinates U = t - r*, V = t + r*.
notation_and_conventions.notes: The same letters mean different things in Example 26.3 and §26.2: in Rindler U, V are the rescaled (Kruskal-like) coordinates, in Schwarzschild they are the unrescaled ones. Worth disambiguating for learners.

notation_and_conventions.convention: Outgoing light has u (or U) constant; incoming light has v (or V) constant. 'Incoming EF' uses (V, r); 'outgoing EF' uses (U, r).
notation_and_conventions.notes: Other texts call these advanced/retarded or ingoing/outgoing and sometimes use v for the ingoing chart.

notation_and_conventions.convention: r* = r + 2M ln|r/2M - 1| with the additive constant set to zero.
Figures use tbar = V - r (incoming chart) or tbar = U + r (outgoing chart) as the vertical axis so the regular null family appears at 45 degrees.
notation_and_conventions.notes: tbar is a plotting device, not the Schwarzschild t.

notation_and_conventions.convention: E-tilde and L-tilde denote energy and angular momentum per unit mass; E-tilde = -u_t = -u_V = -u_U depending on chart.

margin_notes.summary: Boxed reader-route note: this chapter and the next are about coordinate technicalities, and readers after black-hole physics can skip ahead to Chapter 28.
Epigraph from William Blake about perception and seeing the infinite through narrow chinks, a nod to limited coordinate views of an infinite geometry.
Footnote 1: trapped surfaces arose in singularity discussions, but having one does not by itself guarantee a singularity; it only makes one likely.
Footnote 2: the toy examples follow Wald's treatment, where more detail can be found.
Footnote 3: coordinate singularities frequently mean several overlapping coordinate patches are required to cover a spacetime region.

Footnote 4: reminder of the Schwarzschild line element plus the freely falling orthonormal-frame Riemann components (magnitudes 2M/r^3 and M/r^3), pointing out they are finite at r = 2M but blow up at r = 0.
Footnote 5: why a scalar is used: its value is the same in every coordinate system, so its divergence signals real physics.

Footnote 6 (lost from the page export, recovered from the PDF): straight geodesics y = m x + c parametrized by x, showing completeness as t -> 0 and a finite-parameter end as t -> infinity from either side of lambda = -c/m.
Footnote 7 (number lost in export): recap of Minkowski light-cone coordinates u = t - x, v = t + x, the non-diagonal form -du dv, and how the two null families tile flat space.
Footnote 8 (attached to 'Rindler spacetime'): refers back to Chapter 5 for a drawing of the light-cone structure of the Rindler metric.
Footnote 9: expresses Rindler x and t in terms of final Minkowski X and T, remarking that no one would have guessed these without the null-coordinate route.
Footnote 10: recalls the tortoise coordinate from Chapter 25 and fixes its additive constant to zero.
Footnote 11: short biography of David Finkelstein (1929-2016), including ball lightning, Durer's Melencolia I, and naming the sine-Gordon model as a joke.
Footnote 12: in EF coordinates the angular momentum per unit mass is still conserved, and energy per unit mass is now -u_V because the metric does not depend on V.
Footnote 13: Example 26.7 follows the approach of the problem book by Lightman et al.
Footnote 14: since t = U + r* and the receiver sits at fixed position, intervals in t and U coincide there.

difficulty.notes: Algebra is mostly substitution, integration of 1/(1 - 2M/r) and a 2x2 matrix inverse, but Example 26.7 involves a root choice, index raising with cross terms and near-horizon asymptotics. Conceptually it is demanding: separating coordinate artefacts from physics, understanding chart extension, and interpreting tilted light cones. Terse spots and printed slips (sign in 26.26, factor in 26.43, 'V = r = const', 'light that comes from the observer', 'Rinder') can trip novices; the page export also scrambles footnotes 6-8 and mislabels Riemann indices.
